title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR officer still needs judgment; PLAC grade already lost
pass_a_gloss: GAR: you cannot say that by the fall itself man dropped holiness and justice so no judicial stripping was needed—a royal officer who raises war against the King and leaves city, province, and realm likewise falls from the office he bore, yet is still formally abdicated by the King's later judgment. Placeus: he altogether deserves deprivation and that the office be conferred on another, which needs the King's sentence—else another cannot lawfully be adorned with it, and the officer would still be held to retain the post. Raising war and leaving a province is not yet being deprived; sometimes the judicial sentence is deferred. But what is that to the point? Adam by falling already left the grade of obedience and justice in which he stood.
pass_b_english: GAR. Nor is there room for you to say that man by this very thing—that he fell—fell from his holiness and justice, and so there was no need of God's judicial action to strip him of these gifts. What then? Does not also a royal officer who by raising war against the King leaves city, province, kingdom, by that very thing fall from the office he had formerly borne—and yet is none the less by the King's subsequent judgment abdicated from his office? PLAC. He altogether falls from the office—that is, he has deserved to be deprived of the office, and that the same office be conferred on another: for which the King's sentence is needed; otherwise it would not be lawful to adorn another with that office. For that royal officer would still be held to retain his office. For it is one thing to raise war and leave city or province, another to be deprived of office: and so sometimes, such a crime being committed, the judicial sentence is deferred for some time, during which such an officer is not yet held to have lost his office. But what is this to the matter? Have I not shown that by this very thing—that Adam fell—he fell from the grade of obedience and justice in which he formerly was?
source_text: GAR. Neque est quod dicas, hominem eo ipso quod lapsus est, excidisse sua sanctitate & justitia, adeoque nihil opus fuisse actione Dei judiciaria, ut his donis spoliaretur. Quid enim? Non & Regius officiarius, qui bello adversus Regem suscitando, urbe, provincia, Regno excedit, eo ipso excidit illo quod antea gesserat munere: nec tamen eo minus consequenti Regis judicio abdicatur officio suo. PLAC. Omnino excidit munere, hoc est, commeritus est ut munere privetur, idemque munus in alium conferatur: quam ad rem opus est Regis sententia: alioqui non liceret eo munere alium ornare. Censeretur enim is Regius officiarius suum illud munus adhuc retinere. Aliud enim est bellum suscitare, urbe, aut provincia excedere, aliud munere privari: Et sic nonnunquam admisso eiusmodi crimine, ut ad aliquod tempus differatur sententia judiciaria, quo tempore eiusmodi officiarius nondum amisisse suum munus censetur. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Nonne enim ostendi, hoc ipso quod Adamus lapsus est, excidisse eum ex gradu, in quo antea erat, obedientiae & justitiae?
